chunks.section: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
chunks.text: Yanlin Long ynlinlong@gmail.com Affiliation: Independent Researcher Affiliation: Guizhou, China

Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton–Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton–Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton–Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four. † † shortheadings: Finite-Depth Newton–Schulz Dynamics / Long † † firstpage: 1 † † heading: 2026 1–
Newton–Schulz iteration, Gaussian initialization, optimization dynamics, rank selection, saddle avoidance

Muon and its variants have emerged as practical optimizers for large-scale language-model training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team, 2025 ) , using Newton–Schulz iterations to approximately orthogonalize matrix-valued updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . Their design is closely related to steepest descent under the spectral norm, where the polar factor provides an idealized update direction ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . In practice, however, orthogonalization is performed by a fixed, small number of polynomial iterations. This distinction is particularly relevant near rank deficiency: exact polar orthogonalization maps every nonzero singular value to one, whereas finite Newton–Schulz iterations have a bounded amplification factor near zero at each fixed depth. Analyses of idealized spectral updates have identified learning dynamics distinct from gradient descent in concrete matrix models ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Rhee et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , while finite Newton–Schulz updates have been studied through convergence guarantees and their smoothing effect ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Li and Tsuchiya, 2026 ) . These developments motivate a direct study of how the finite number of iterations shapes the optimization trajectory.

Polynomial iterations for matrix orthogonalization have a long history in numerical linear algebra ( Kovarik, 1970 ; Björck and Bowie, 1971 ; Higham, 1986 ; Higham and Schreiber, 1990 ) . More recently, optimization analyses that explicitly retain finitely many Newton–Schulz iterations have investigated convergence to stationary points, the dependence on iteration depth, and the effects of stabilization and momentum ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Li and Tsuchiya, 2026 ; Peng et al., 2026 ; Li and Tan, 2026 ) . These results provide a useful foundation for studying the dynamical consequences of a fixed-depth spectral transformation.

Gradient-based training of factorized models from small initialization can exhibit incremental learning, with different components becoming appreciable at successive stages ( Saxe et al., 2014 ; Jacot et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Berthier, 2023 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . In matrix factorization, this behavior can take the form of dominant directions being learned first, followed by weaker directions that increase the effective rank of the predictor. The trajectory may consequently pass near intermediate low-rank stationary points. Related analyses of homogeneous networks describe directional convergence near the origin and saddle points, as well as the subsequent trajectory toward the first saddle after escape ( Kumar and Haupt, 2024 ; Kumar and Haupt, 2025 ) . A complementary approach studies training dynamics in high-dimensional limits, extracting effective structure from the evolving parameters or deriving dynamical mean-field descriptions of gradient flow ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Martin et al., 2026 ) . Related work on feature learning and the distinction from lazy training provides another perspective on how different directions become accessible during optimization ( Chizat et al., 2019 ; Dandi et al., 2024 ) . Since Newton–Schulz iterations amplify small singular values of the normalized gradient, a natural question is whether a finite increase in the number of iterations can make weaker directions emerge early enough to change which stationary points the trajectory approaches. Answering this question requires tracking both singular-value amplification and the coupled evolution of different directions, as the gradient and its singular subspaces evolve with the factorized parameters.

We consider a two-layer neural network with quadratic activation and all second-layer weights fixed to one. This model admits an equivalent representation as a positive-semidefinite matrix factorization. Such quadratic networks provide a tractable setting for analyzing nonlinear training dynamics, and have also been studied through gradient flow and spectral gradient methods ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Martin et al., 2026 ; Braun et al., 2026 ) . We study continuous-time optimization dynamics in which K K cubic Newton–Schulz iterations are applied to the normalized factor gradient, and refer to K K as the spectral depth. For the analysis, we use a two-scale Gaussian initialization: one hidden row is initialized at scale ε \varepsilon , while the remaining rows have scale ε b \varepsilon^{b} , where b > 1 b>1 . The gradient normalization includes an additive stabilization proportional to ε \varepsilon . This choice of initialization scales allows us to identify the leading directional dynamics first and then derive the coupled equations governing the weaker components in the remaining independent directions. We compare trajectories on the same task and with the same underlying Gaussian seed as ε \varepsilon tends to zero, while keeping each spectral depth fixed. Removing the row-dependent initialization scales would instead lead to an isotropic Gaussian initialization, for which the competing directions may exhibit different and potentially richer dynamics. The analysis of this regime remains open.

Another question concerns the extent to which small-initialization asymptotics can determine the subsequent training trajectory. Under suitable structural conditions, gradient flow admits a precise description in which the initialization scale can be used to reverse-engineer the full training dynamics, leading also to a characterization of time-dependent implicit regularization ( Berthier, 2023 ) . For finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics, the nonlinear matrix iteration prevents this reconstruction argument from carrying over directly. Although the dynamics can be analyzed in a small neighborhood of the origin, the resulting local description does not by itself determine the trajectory after leaving that neighborhood. This creates two distinct dynamical scales: the entrance dynamics near the origin and the subsequent evolution away from it. Establishing how the entrance dynamics are transmitted to the later trajectory is one of the main results of this paper.

Following the framework of Li et al. (2021) , which characterizes the first nonzero stationary point selected by gradient flow under suitable assumptions, we study the evolution from small initialization through the first stationary point encountered after escape. This allows us to compare the stationary points approached by gradient descent and by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics. Under an additional structural assumption, we establish a sufficient large-depth guarantee: for all sufficiently large spectral depths, the selected Newton–Schulz continuation approaches a first stationary point whose loss is strictly smaller than that of the first stationary point selected by gradient descent. For smaller depths, our results do not provide a general criterion determining whether the trajectory visits or bypasses the gradient-descent stationary point. Moreover, without the additional assumption, the first stationary points reached by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics and gradient descent may have the same loss. Such equal-loss behavior may reveal further dynamical structures, which we leave for future work. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and pathwise comparison criteria. Sections 3–5 establish the Gaussian entrance law, continuation criteria, and eventual depth guarantee. Section 6 presents an exact empirical task, and Section 7 discusses the scope of the results and open questions. Detailed proofs are given in the appendices.

chunks.section: 3 Gaussian Entrance at Finite Spectral Depth
chunks.text: An independent weak component can be suppressed during one stage and amplified during a later stage. The entrance rank records how many such components reach a fixed rescaled size before physical time becomes independent of initialization. This section first gives the finite recursion computing that rank, then identifies its limit in the actual Gaussian dynamics.

Lines between integer depths guide the eye; the polar reference is displayed separately.

In this paper, we have studied how finitely many iterations of a nonlinear matrix transformation can reshape optimization dynamics. In a quadratic two-layer network, we have characterized the evolution from small-initialization escape near the origin to the first nonzero stationary stage. Our results provide a precise description of how the number of Newton–Schulz iterations controls early rank selection and regulates the subsequent optimization path. Beyond this particular model, the analysis offers a framework combining spectral dynamics with small-initialization techniques, which may help understand certain training phenomena arising in large-scale neural networks, including language models. An immediate open question is whether similar dynamical descriptions can be established for more general models and under weaker assumptions. Of particular interest are networks with nonlinear activations such as ReLU, high-dimensional training regimes, and deeper architectures, where the interaction between spectral updates and feature learning may lead to richer dynamics.

chunks.section: A.3 Cited analytic tools and the normalized leading-direction limit
chunks.text: Local solution, uniqueness, dependence, and continuation results are used in the forms of Teschl (2012, Theorems 2.2, 2.9, 2.11, 2.13 and Corollary 2.15) . At each application the vector field is locally Lipschitz on the indicated region, and compact confinement extends the solution as needed. The integral comparison is Teschl (2012, Lemma 2.7) ; the nonhomogeneous form follows by including the accumulated forcing in the additive term and interchanging the integrals. For measurable coefficients the integrating-factor argument applies to absolutely continuous primitives. The weighted function spaces used below are Banach spaces after multiplication by their displayed weight. Each application of Teschl (2012, Theorem 2.1) verifies invariance of a closed ball and a strict contraction estimate. Nonzero determinant polynomials have null zero sets by Mityagin (2020) ; an identity submatrix witnesses their nontriviality, and Gaussian density transfers nullity to probability zero. The next lemma states the normalization of the local exit result needed in the empirical passage argument. Its proof retains the asymptotic, uniqueness, and compact-interval comparison steps around the cited shifted-limit theorem.
